narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 76.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction, offering a modest pull toward passing.

In simple terms, the model saw that you finished both your first and third years in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average student who was accepted, who typically ranked around the middle of their class. These consistently low relative performances outweighed the positive signal from your LSAT score and other details.

Your family income and plan to attend full-time were not major drivers of the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance to the middle or upper part of your class in the remaining years. Stronger grades that move you out of the lowest decile would likely change the model’s prediction and open future opportunities. Consider seeking academic support now so your record shows clear upward progress.
